summary: A Next.js route handler called the repo's REAL writeReviewStatus (lock -> fresh read inside the lock -> validate -> atomic write) via runtime dynamic import; nothing was reimplemented. notes: ⚠️ HOST EXECUTION, stated rather than implied. The tier-1 controller could not run this at all: the job declares `requires: { network: true }` for `npm install` and the approved ceiling refuses it before provisioning (#77), and — separately and more fundamentally — the job model has no form for a long-lived service alongside commands, so the probe is not expressible under it regardless of the ceiling. See the capability gap recorded as its own question. ⚠️ Controls before AND after the treatment, so 'no interference' is a comparison rather than an assertion: a second control isolates interference from any second-run effect. ⚠️ The workspace was removed and its ABSENCE checked rather than the removal call trusted — the same discipline the controller uses, applied by hand because no controller ran. ⚠️ METHODOLOGY HISTORY — AN INVALIDATED FIRST RUN, EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED FROM THE FINDING ABOVE. An earlier execution of this probe reported treatment 0/20 with the controls at 20/20, which read as total interference from `next dev`. It was a FIXTURE DEFECT, not an observation: both runs wrote the same filenames into the same directory, so the control created the files and the treatment only modified them, while the watcher listened for `add`. A second defect in the same version measured latency as elapsed-time-since-watcher-start, which reports the write schedule (20 files x 120ms) rather than detection lag and would have read as ~2.4s of latency on a completely idle watcher. ⚠️ NONE OF THAT RUN'S NUMBERS CONTRIBUTE ANYTHING HERE. They are void rather than weak, and the summary, outcome and omissions above describe only the corrected execution: a fresh directory per run, per-file observed-minus-written latency, and a control taken after the treatment as well as before. Both defects were in the fixture; neither touched the code under observation. ⚠️ It is preserved because the correction is WHY this result can be trusted rather than a detail about how it was obtained. The control is what exposed it — a result that dramatic, from a change that small, is a bug before it is a finding — and a probe whose only reported run is the one that worked has not demonstrated that it could have failed.

No file was missed in any run, and `next dev` did not recompile during the content writes.

notes: ⚠️ TWO INSTRUMENT DEFECTS were found and corrected before these numbers were trusted, and both would have read as findings. (1) The marker extractor sliced between two sentinels in the HTML; under Cache Components the Suspense fallback ships in the static shell and the value STREAMS, so the first match landed inside escaped RSC flight data and both Cache Components runs scored 'inconclusive' while plainly serving the right value. Replaced with sentinel presence, which is immune to escaping because only one sentinel is on disk at a time. (2) The route-symbol matcher did not know `◐` (partially prerendered), so it fell through and reported `○ /_not-found` as the route under test. Both defects were in the instrument, not in Next.js. ⚠️ The baseline was re-run in the same pass as the corrected variants rather than carried over from the earlier pass, so every row here was measured by ONE instrument.
summary: Seven distinct mechanism/caching-model combinations built and served under `next build` + `next start`, each measured by writing a different value to the artifact after the server was live and re-requesting. Results: baseline/cacheComponents:false -> ┌ ○ / frozen; baseline/cacheComponents:true -> ┌ ○ / frozen; connection/cacheComponents:false -> ┌ ƒ / FRESH; connection/cacheComponents:true -> BUILD FAILED; force-dynamic/cacheComponents:false -> ┌ ƒ / FRESH; baseline/cacheComponents:false -> ┌ ○ / frozen; baseline/cacheComponents:true -> ┌ ○ / frozen; connection-suspense/cacheComponents:false -> ┌ ƒ / FRESH; connection-suspense/cacheComponents:true -> ┌ ◐ / FRESH; io-suspense/cacheComponents:false -> ┌ ○ / frozen; io-suspense/cacheComponents:true -> ┌ ◐ / FRESH. Only `connection()` behind a Suspense boundary reflected the external write in BOTH caching models.
title: Experiment: which freshness mechanisms survive a production build

notes: ⚠️ THIS IS NOT A RE-RUN OF EVD-0023, and the difference is the point. EVD-0023 compared MECHANISMS, one read per build, to choose one. This measures the CONTRACT AS WRITTEN — `connection()` before EACH read, a fallback that is a real loading state — and it carries a NEGATIVE CONTROL inside the same build. Without the control, a fresh result would not distinguish the contract doing the work from something incidental about the build. The control was stale in both configurations, so the contract is load-bearing rather than decorative. ⚠️ THE CONTROL INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCES AST-0019 a third time, in a third instrument: `○ /bare` built static and served build-time content with cacheComponents both enabled and disabled. ⚠️ THE MIXED ROUTE IS THE FINDING NOBODY ASKED FOR. Its non-compliant read came back FRESH in both configurations, because a compliant sibling had already made the route dynamic. See AST-0022 — it is the reason the 'each read' clause is not redundant.
summary: One application, three routes, built and served twice under `next build` + `next start`. The contract route makes two planning-content reads, each awaiting `connection()` inside its own Suspense boundary with a named loading fallback. The control route makes the same read with neither. A third route mixes one of each. Copies of real planning artifacts were read through `JSON.parse(readFileSync(...))` and a markdown read, then rewritten externally with the server live. With cacheComponents DISABLED the routes built as "┌ ƒ /", "└ ƒ /mixed" and "├ ○ /bare"; with it ENABLED, "┌ ◐ /", "└ ◐ /mixed" and "├ ○ /bare". In BOTH configurations the contract route served the externally written values on every request after the write, its Suspense fallback was present in the initial HTML, and the control route served its build-time values on every request including five seconds later. The mixed route served BOTH slots fresh — including the non-compliant one.
title: Experiment: the DEC-0019 read contract, with a non-compliant control on the same build

omissions.reason: Five forbidden constructs were exercised: import/export, flow and text expressions, JSX attribute expressions, spread attributes, and unmapped components. notes: ⚠️ TWO CONFIGURATION CONSTRAINTS WERE MEASURED, and both first presented as the contract failing. (1) Next.js 16.3.2 builds with TURBOPACK by default, which serialises the config — so a remark plugin must be given as a module path, not a function reference. (2) That path must be ABSOLUTE: `@next/mdx` resolves a relative path with `require.resolve(p, {paths:[projectRoot]})` from its own package directory, so `./lib/plugin.mjs` fails with `Cannot find module` and a require stack rooted in `node_modules/@next/mdx`. That message reads like a broken plugin rather than a configuration rule, and it cost a build to tell apart. ⚠️ REJECT, NOT STRIP, is what makes the diagnostics possible at all. `file.fail` carries the node's position; a stripping plugin has nothing to report because by construction nothing is wrong afterwards.
summary: One `@next/mdx` application, a remark plugin that calls `file.fail` on forbidden nodes, and six documents built through `next build`. accept: built ✓; reject-import: refused @ 1:1 ✓; reject-expression: refused @ 3:8 ✓; reject-attr-expression: refused @ 3:10 ✓; reject-spread: refused @ 3:10 ✓; reject-unmapped: refused @ 3:1 ✓. The accepted document built as a route, rendered its markdown, and rendered the mapped component. Each of the five refusals failed the build and named the file with a line:column position and a reason.

facts.analysis: static, text only; no application code executed

omissions.reason: `import(someVariable)` cannot be followed by a text analysis. It is DETECTED and reported as an unfollowable import, and the lint exits non-zero on one, so the blind spot is loud rather than silent — but a specifier that is computed cannot be resolved without running the code.

Only relative specifiers are resolved; a bare specifier is treated as a package. If a path alias (`@/lib/...`) is ever configured, the analyser would treat it as external and miss it. No alias is configured today.
This task covers the import boundary only. The planning-read and `<Suspense>` half is TSK-0015, and ACC-0024 needs both.

notes: ⚠️ THE FIXTURES CAUGHT TWO REAL BUGS BEFORE THE CHECK WAS TRUSTED, which is the argument for writing them first. (1) Every violation was reported ONE LINE EARLY: the pattern consumes the character before `import`/`export` so a specifier inside an identifier cannot match, and that character is usually the previous line's newline. The transitive fixture caught it because its violation is deliberately not on line 1. (2) A lazy `[\s\S]*?` let a side-effect `import "server-only";` run on to the NEXT statement's `from` clause, attributing that specifier to the wrong line and swallowing the statement between them. ⚠️ A THIRD DEFECT WAS FOUND BY RUNNING IT, not by a fixture: the first version scoped the check to modules REACHABLE from a route, and since no view imports the reader yet it walked two files and reported the project clean without looking at the reader or either adapter. Scope is now every module under `app/`; reachability only supplies the chain.
summary: A static analyser was built that reads application modules as text and never executes them. Run against three fixtures: the ALLOWED case (a page reaching `lib/` through an adapter) reported no violations while confirming the adapter was actually walked; the DIRECT case (a page importing `lib/` itself) was reported at `app/page.js:1`; the TRANSITIVE case (a page importing an innocent-looking helper that re-exports `lib/`) was reported at `app/_helpers/shim.js:2` — the file whose import statement is the violation — with the chain `app/page.js → app/_helpers/shim.js`. Run against the real project it reports no violations over 5 scanned modules. Falsified in real application code twice: a direct `lib/` import added to the reader was reported at `app/_read/planning.js:3` with exit 1, and a transitive one through a new `app/_helpers/shim.js` was reported at that file's line 1, also exit 1.
title: Experiment: the import-boundary check, falsified against fixtures and against real code

facts.analysis: static, text only; no application code executed

omissions.reason: No module in the real application consumes the reader yet — the lint reports `0 reader consumer(s)`. The two boundary detectors therefore have nothing to examine there and were falsified against temporary real-code violations and against fixtures instead. They begin covering real code at TSK-0007.

A component's enclosure is judged where it is RENDERED by name. A component passed as a prop, rendered through a variable, or wrapped by a boundary in a parent layout rather than at the call site would not be judged correctly. No such pattern exists yet; it is a real limit rather than a hypothetical one.
Unchanged from the import half: a computed specifier cannot be resolved by text, and the lint exits non-zero on one rather than passing over it.

notes: ⚠️ THE FIXTURES CAUGHT THREE DEFECTS, TWO OF THEM IN THE FIXTURES THEMSELVES. (1) The fixture components imported the reader with `../_read/planning` from `app/`, which climbs OUT of the app directory — so nothing resolved, `consumers` was empty, and the ALLOWED case reported clean for the worst possible reason. The `consumers.length > 0` assertion is what caught it, and it was written for exactly that. (2) A `sed` fix then broke the indirect fixture's path in the other direction. (3) In the analyser, two `new RegExp` template literals lost a backslash level, so `await\s+` became `awaits+` and matched nothing — a detector that silently could not fire. ⚠️ FIXTURES ARE `.jsx` BECAUSE `node --test` COLLECTS `.js` UNDER `test/`, and these contain JSX that Node cannot parse. Collected, they failed the suite for a reason unrelated to what they test. `.jsx` sits outside the runner's patterns and inside the analyser's.
summary: A second static analysis was added: it scans every module under `app/`, asserts the designated reader exists and was examined, and emits four kinds of violation. Six fixtures, one per detected violation plus an allowed control: ALLOWED reported clean with a consumer present; DIRECT caught a component importing an adapter at line 1; INDIRECT caught a helper re-exporting the adapter at its own line 1, not at the page that used it; MISSING-BOUNDARY caught `<Panel>` rendered bare at the rendering site, line 3; FS-DIRECT caught `node:fs` at line 1; ROUTE-READ caught a route entry awaiting the reader at line 3. Each of the four detectors was then falsified again against a TEMPORARY violation inserted into the real application, and each reported the real file and line before being reverted. A missing reader is reported as `readerSeen: false` rather than as a clean project.
title: Experiment: read and `<Suspense>` confinement, four detectors falsified twice over
